If admitting the request would exceed the quota, the request is throttled with an HTTP 429 response.\\n2. **Output tokens per minute** \u2013 As the model streams or generates output, output tokens are counted against the output-tokens-per-minute quota for that model. If the quota is reached during generation, generation stops and the response is returned with a finish reason indicating the cutoff.\\n\\nAfter the response completes, any unused portion of the initial input-token reservation (the difference between `max_tokens` and the actual output) is replenished to your quota.\\n\\nThe endpoint may apply additional internal rate limiting that is not exposed in Service Quotas. Use retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient throttling.\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint's TPM quotas count input and output tokens together against a single per-model quota, while the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint applies separate input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas. If you run workloads on both endpoints, plan capacity for each endpoint independently. For details on the runtime endpoint's quotas, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock\",\"context\":\"# How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock\\n\\nWhen you run model inference, there are quotas on the number of tokens that can be processed depending on which Amazon Bedrock model you use. Token count is estimated based on on-demand pricing; actual token consumption varies by model, input/output ratio, and cache usage. |\\n| `max_tokens` | A parameter you provide in your request to set a maximum amount of output tokens the model can generate. |\\n| Burndown rate | The rate at which input and output tokens are converted into token quota usage for the throttling system. |\\n\\nThe burndown rate for Anthropic Claude models version 4.8 is **15x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 15 tokens from your quotas) and the burndown rate for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Fable 5.2 is **10x for output tokens**. The burndown rate for Anthropic Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and Claude\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"GPT-6.1 Sol\",\"context\":\"## Quotas and Limits\\n\\nQuotas vary by account and Region. See Quotas for Amazon Bedrock and the model's service quota settings.\\n\\nThe output-token burndown rate is 10: each output token consumes 10 tokens of quota\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-openai-gpt-6-1-sol.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"GPT-6.2 Sol\",\"context\":\"## Quotas and Limits\\n\\nQuotas vary by account and Region. See Quotas for Amazon Bedrock and the model's service quota settings.\\n\\nThe output-token burndown rate is 10: each output token consumes 10 tokens of quota\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-openai-gpt-6-2-sol.html\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"Scaling and throughput best practices\",\"context\":\"## `bedrock-runtime` endpoint: throughput and quotas\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint has the following quota behavior:\\n\\n* Per-model, per-Region token quotas count input and output tokens together. Output tokens consume quota according to a model-specific burndown rate.\\n* Some models also have RPM quotas, while other models are governed only by token quotas. Allocations for `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle` are independent.\\n* Custom inference profiles, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput have separate quotas and are available only through `bedrock-runtime`.\\n\\nFor current quota values, token-burndown details, and the quota-increase process, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See the applicable Models at a glance for model-specific endpoint, service-tier, and feature support\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/scaling-throughput-best-practices.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up Bedrock quota and provisioned throughput guidance"}

Amazon Bedrock endpoints (char 209-1908)\\n    - Why the two endpoints behave differently (char 1032-1908)\\n  - `bedrock-mantle` endpoint: throughput and quotas (char 1909-3311)\\n  - `bedrock-runtime` endpoint: throughput and quotas (char 3312-4319)\\n  - Understanding HTTP error responses (char 4320-5819)\\n  - Recommended error handling (char 5820-8608)\\n    - Transient errors (char 5851-7825)\\n          - Example Retry configuration for `bedrock-runtime` (AWS SDK / boto3) (char 6844-7104)\\n          - Example Retry configuration for `bedrock-mantle` (OpenAI SDK) (char 7105-7329)\\n          - Example Retry configuration for `bedrock-mantle` (Anthropic SDK) (char 7330-7825)\\n    - Sustained capacity errors (char 7826-8608)\\n  - Ramping up throughput (char 8609-10402)\\n    - Recommended ramp-up procedure (char 8995-10402)\\n  - Additional best practices (char 10403-11164)\\n  - Regional availability and cross-Region inference (char 11165-11674)\\n  - Getting help (char 11675-12426)\\n  - Summary of recommendations (char 12427-13390)\\n\\n# Scaling and throughput best practices\\n\\nThis topic explains how throughput limits and scheduling work across Amazon Bedrock endpoints and provides best practices for scaling your generative AI applications.\\n\\n## Amazon Bedrock endpoints\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock supports two endpoints for inference:\\n\\n* `bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws` \u2014 Supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Anthropic Messages API.\\n* `bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com` \u2014 Supports the Bedrock-native InvokeModel and Converse APIs, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Anthropic Messages API.\\n\\nFor most new applications, start with `bedrock-runtime`. Use `bedrock-mantle` when you need capabilities that are available only on that endpoint, such as server-side tools, background inference, Projects, Workspaces, or a model that is available only on `bedrock-mantle`. You can use both endpoints in the same application. For a complete comparison, see Inference endpoints supported by Amazon Bedrock.\\n\\n### Why the two endpoints behave differently\\n\\nBoth endpoint surfaces use the same underlying inference engine, but their quota accounting and capacity options differ. bedrock-runtime uses per-model token quotas and, for some models, requests-per-minute (RPM) quotas. bedrock-mantle does not enforce RPM quotas and uses separate input-token and output-token quotas for models that have published quotas. Other models on `bedrock-mantle` might not have per-account quotas exposed in Service Quotas, but their throughput is still governed by internal service capacity.\\n\\nA quota is an upper bound, not a guarantee that every on-demand request will be served immediately. During periods of high demand, requests can be queued or receive transient capacity errors. Design your application to bound concurrency, queue work, and retry transient errors without creating a retry surge.\\n\\n## `bedrock-mantle` endpoint: throughput and quotas\\n\\nThe `bedrock-mantle` endpoint has the following quota behavior:\\n\\n* Models with published quotas have separate per-model, per-Region input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas.\\n* The endpoint does not enforce RPM quotas. Two workloads with the same RPM can consume very different amounts of capacity, so plan and rate-limit by tokens and concurrency instead of RPM alone.\\n* When a request is admitted, the input-token check includes the input tokens plus the requested `max_tokens` value. After the response completes, the unused part of that reservation is replenished. Set `max_tokens` no higher than your application needs.\\n* Models without published TPM quotas do not currently have per-account TPM quotas exposed in Service Quotas. This does not mean that throughput is unlimited; internal service capacity and transient rate limiting still apply.\\n* Batch inference and Provisioned Throughput are available only through `bedrock-runtime`. Service-tier and model support varies by model.\\n\\nDefault values and your account's allocations can vary by model, Region, and usage history. For current values, quota evaluation details, and the AWS Support process for requesting an increase, see Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint. See the applicable Models at a glance for model-specific endpoint, service-tier, and feature support.\\n\\n## `bedrock-runtime` endpoint: throughput and quotas\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint has the following quota behavior:\\n\\n* Per-model, per-Region token quotas count input and output tokens together. Output tokens consume quota according to a model-specific burndown rate.\\n* Some models also have RPM quotas, while other models are governed only by token quotas. Check the quotas that apply to the exact model and inference profile that you use.\\n* Per-minute and per-day token quotas are shared across the inference APIs that call the same model on this endpoint. Allocations for `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle` are independent.\\n* Custom inference profiles, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput have separate quotas and are available only through `bedrock-runtime`.\\n\\nFor current quota values, token-burndown details, and the quota-increase process, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See the applicable Models at a glance for model-specific endpoint, service-tier, and feature support.\\n\\n## Understanding HTTP error responses\\n\\nHTTP 429\\n:   A 429 response means that the request was not admitted. Inspect the API-specific error type rather than relying on the HTTP status alone. A `ThrottlingException` or rate-limit error generally means that the request exceeded an account quota or a service rate limit. Some runtime operations also use HTTP 429 for `ModelNotReadyException`. On `bedrock-mantle`, check input and output TPM usage and the request's `max_tokens` value; the endpoint does not have an RPM quota. On `bedrock-runtime`, check combined token quotas and RPM, if the model has an RPM quota.\\n\\nHTTP 503\\n:   A 503 response means that the service is temporarily unable to handle the request because of high demand or a capacity constraint. It does not indicate that you exceeded an account quota. Retry transient responses with exponential backoff and jitter. If the response persists, stop increasing traffic, reduce concurrency, and consider a different Region or cross-Region inference when supported.\\n\\nHTTP 529 (`overloaded_error`)\\n:   Some model APIs return 529 when the model is temporarily unable to process the request because of high demand or insufficient serving capacity. Treat it as a transient capacity error. If the response includes a `Retry-After` header, wait for at least that duration before retrying, and add jitter so that clients do not retry simultaneously.\\n\\nFor API-specific causes and resolution steps, see Troubleshooting Amazon Bedrock API Error Codes.\\n\\n## Recommended error handling\\n\\n### Transient errors\\n\\nRetry only errors that are safe to retry, such as transient throttling and capacity errors. If the service returns a `Retry-After` header, honor it. Otherwise, implement exponential backoff with random jitter:\\n\\n* Start with a short delay (for example, 1 second).\\n* Increase the delay after each retry and cap the maximum delay to fit your application's latency budget.\\n* Add random jitter and avoid synchronized retries across workers.\\n* Use a bounded retry budget that fits your application's latency objective. For example, limit the operation to six total attempts: the initial request and up to five retries.\\n\\nMost AWS SDKs and popular HTTP libraries provide built-in support for this pattern. Retry-setting names differ: botocore's `total_max_attempts` includes the initial request, while the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs' `max_retries` counts only retries. The following examples therefore use different numeric values to provide the same example six-attempt budget.\\n\\n###### Example Retry configuration for `bedrock-runtime` (AWS SDK / boto3)\\n\\n```\\nimport boto3\\nfrom botocore.config import Config\\n\\nconfig = Config(retries={\\\"total_max_attempts\\\": 6, \\\"mode\\\": \\\"standard\\\"})\\nclient = boto3.client(\\\"bedrock-runtime\\\", config=config)\\n```\\n\\n###### Example Retry configuration for `bedrock-mantle` (OpenAI SDK)\\n\\n```\\nfrom openai import OpenAI\\n\\nclient = OpenAI(\\n    api_key=api_key,\\n    base_url=f\\\"https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/v1\\\",\\n    max_retries=5,\\n)\\n```\\n\\n###### Example Retry configuration for `bedrock-mantle` (Anthropic SDK)\\n\\n```\\nimport anthropic\\n\\nclient = anthropic.Anthropic(\\n    api_key=api_key,\\n    base_url=f\\\"https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/anthropic\\\",\\n    max_retries=5,\\n)\\n```\\n\\nConfigure connection and read timeouts separately from retries, based on the model and operation's documented maximum inference duration. A timeout that is shorter than a valid long-running inference request can cause avoidable retries and duplicate work.\\n\\n### Sustained capacity errors\\n\\nIf you receive persistent 503 or 529 errors, retries alone can amplify load. The service might be experiencing a temporary capacity constraint, or the workload might exceed the capacity currently available for the model and Region. Take the following steps:\\n\\n* Stop the ramp and return to the last stable request rate and concurrency level.\\n* Use bounded client-side concurrency, rate limiting, and request queues.\\n* Defer or shed lower-priority requests until capacity recovers.\\n* For `bedrock-runtime`, use cross-Region inference when the model supports it. For predictable, sustained workloads, evaluate Provisioned Throughput.\\n* If the problem continues, check the AWS Health Dashboard and contact AWS Support with request IDs and UTC timestamps.\\n\\n## Ramping up throughput\\n\\nOn-demand capacity can vary by model, Region, and time. Not all requests within a quota are guaranteed to succeed during periods of high demand, so ramp gradually when launching a workload, changing models or Regions, or making a large traffic increase. This is especially important for `bedrock-mantle` models that do not have a published per-account quota.\\n\\n### Recommended ramp-up procedure\\n\\n1. Estimate the target token rate and concurrency for each endpoint, model, and Region. For `bedrock-mantle`, track input and output tokens separately and include the requested `max_tokens` value in the input-token admission estimate.\\n2. Begin at a known stable baseline below the target. If you do not have a baseline, start with a small representative load instead of sending the full target volume.\\n3. Hold each level long enough to observe request success, 429/503/529 errors, latency percentiles, token consumption, concurrency, and queue depth.\\n4. Increase one controlled step at a time. Change only one major load dimension at a time so that you can identify the cause of a regression.\\n5. If throttling, capacity errors, or latency rise beyond your threshold, pause the ramp, honor any `Retry-After` header, and return to the last stable level.\\n6. Continue until you reach the target, and repeat the validation for every model and Region that will receive product\",\"total_length\":13391,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":10000,\"truncated\":true,\"redirected_url\":null,\"error_code\":null}]}}"}]}], "label": "Read Bedrock scaling and throughput best practices page"}

**What I found**
- This account in us-east-1 has no `InvocationThrottles` metric in the last ~2 weeks. Either the throttling is in another Region or account, or it is older than that.
- I did see Bedrock traffic on several models here. They include `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5`, `us.openai.gpt-5.6-terra`, Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and some Nova and Titan models.
- Which model is throttling, and in which Region, decides the answer.

**Which option fits**

| Your situation | Better fit |
|---|---|
| Throttling is brief, around peaks, and average usage is well below the quota | Quota increase, plus retries and smoothing |
| Load is sustained and predictable, with a steady baseline close to the limit | Provisioned Throughput |
| Latency or availability must be guaranteed for a critical path | Provisioned Throughput |
| Spiky or unpredictable traffic | Quota increase and cross-Region inference. Provisioned Throughput is billed for committed capacity whether or not you use it. |

**Try these first, since they're free**
1. **Check the burndown rate.** On `bedrock-runtime`, input and output tokens count together against one per-model quota. Output tokens burn down faster. Per the docs, Claude 4.8 uses 15x and several newer models use 10x. A request with a large output can use far more quota than its raw token count suggests.
2. **Lower `max_tokens`.** Admission checks reserve input tokens plus `max_tokens`. Oversized values cause throttling even when actual usage is low.
3. **Use cross-Region inference profiles** where the model supports them. The `us.*` models you're already using are in this group.
4. **Add exponential backoff with jitter and bounded concurrency.** Also queue or shed low-priority work at peak, for example by moving it to batch.
5. **Distinguish 429 from 503/529.** A 429 means you hit your quota, so an increase helps. A 503 or 529 is a service capacity problem. A quota increase won't fix it, and Provisioned Throughput or another Region might.

**Quota increase vs. Provisioned Throughput**
- A quota increase is free and usually the first thing to try. It raises the ceiling but isn't a capacity guarantee, because the docs say on-demand requests within quota can still see transient capacity errors at high demand.
- Provisioned Throughput is only available on `bedrock-runtime`. It has its own quotas, and not every model supports it.

If you tell me the model ID, Region and account, I can pull peak token usage and throttle counts for the last 1 to 2 weeks. I'd compare them against your Service Quotas values.
